snapshots.name: The Division of Labour
snapshots.subtitle: Book I's opening argument
snapshots.body: The principle the book opens with: that the greatest improvements in productive power come from splitting a task into simple, repeated operations — illustrated by the famous example of a pin-maker's workshop, where ten specialized workers vastly outproduce ten generalists.

snapshots.name: Self-Interest and the Invisible Hand
snapshots.subtitle: Why the butcher feeds you
snapshots.body: Smith's account of how self-interested exchange coordinates society without anyone intending the public good: we get our dinner not from the butcher's kindness but from his regard to his own interest, and the individual pursuing only his own gain is led by an invisible hand toward an end no part of his intention.

snapshots.name: Natural Price and Market Price
snapshots.subtitle: Chapter VII's distinction
snapshots.body: The distinction that anchors Smith's theory of value: the natural price a commodity tends toward when rent, wages, and profit are all paid at their ordinary rates, against the market price it actually and commonly sells for, which can rise above or fall below that natural level.

snapshots.name: Wages of Labour
snapshots.subtitle: What labour earns
snapshots.body: The natural recompense of labour, discussed in Chapter VIII: in the earliest state of society the whole produce belongs to the labourer, but once land is appropriated and stock accumulated, wages become a share negotiated between masters and workers.

snapshots.name: The Profits of Stock
snapshots.subtitle: What capital earns
snapshots.body: Chapter IX's subject: the return earned by the owner of accumulated capital, which Smith argues rises and falls with the same causes that move wages — the growing or declining wealth of society — but in the opposite direction.

snapshots.name: Rent of Land
snapshots.subtitle: What landlords earn
snapshots.body: Understood as the price paid for the use of land, discussed in Chapter XI as naturally the highest amount a tenant can be made to pay given the land's actual condition — a payment Smith treats as governed by different laws than wages or profit.

snapshots.name: The Origin and Use of Money
snapshots.subtitle: Chapter IV's subject
snapshots.body: How, once the division of labour was established, the inconvenience of direct barter led every prudent person to keep some commodity on hand that others would readily accept in exchange — the origin, Smith argues, of money as a universal medium of trade.

snapshots.name: The Mercantile System
snapshots.subtitle: The doctrine Smith writes against
snapshots.body: The system of trade policy — export bounties, import restrictions, the equation of national wealth with a favorable balance of trade — that much of the book's later chapters are devoted to dismantling, on the grounds that it enriches particular merchants at the expense of the whole country.
